links.reason: 640 has the kings vow to plunge into war if another takes her (பிறன் வெளவுமேல் கோணைப் போரிற் குளிக்குவம்); 791 shows kings fighting after the contest, which fits that vow rather than breaking it. 791 does not say Civakan won at the vina, so a broken term is read in, not found.

3133 already joins fasting and meditation with reverence to the Tirthan (தீர்த்தன் வந்தியா), so effort and devotion are not split between the two verses as teaches claims. The link is the shared karma-washing theme; 3133's sense is flagged uncertain.

Soolamani 1 says those who bowed at his feet were freed (அடிக்கீழ் பணிந்தார் வினை நீங்கி நின்றார்), so the verse does not credit release only to the conqueror's own victory; the devotee's freedom comes through the feet, close to a grace reading. The contrast with சிவனருளால் வினை சேரகிலாமை is real but a difference of emphasis, not an incompatible claim.

1460 leaves the discus's sparing of the youth unexplained (நேமி ... வலப்புடை நின்றதன்றே); 1463 gives the reason by the simile of a curse ending in the speaker's mouth and the discus killing the king who sent it (தன்னையே செகுத்ததன்றே). The later verse answers the earlier one's puzzle, not mere sequence.

821 has Civakan take the remnant and conch water at the Tirthan's feet; it is an offering remnant, not a pilgrim's bathing in tirtha waters, and nothing says he thinks the water clears his sin. Tirumular's target is wandering to bathe (பள்ளமும் மேடும் திரிவர்), so the note builds a tension from the word தீர்த்தன்/தீர்த்தம் and the marker's own doubt about கூலித்.
links.text_issue: line 2 கூலித் doubtful; sense flagged uncertain

links.reason: Kural 633 lists பிரித்தலும் ... among the minister's skills and 755 has Padumukan say the one left will divide them (வேறு செய்து) and rule when they perish. But 755 never calls him a minister; that identity comes from the story outside the verse, and the 'gains' that Kattiyankaran is practising the minister's art leans on it.

153 has the king and his mother die and enter the animal state (துன்னினாரே); 34 has a brother and sister recall earlier animal births killed by kin. The Tamil does not identify the two pairs, and 34 is the earlier verse in the book, so 'told later' is wrong in text order and the single pair is a plot reconstruction.

273 has the king lay down anger and weapon yet still ask why he should bow to a dust-grimed man (தொழுமாறு அளியன் யாவன்); 283 has him bow with crown-flowers touching the ascetic's feet (சென்னிமுடி துன்னுமலர் அடிகளுற வணங்கி). The later scene reverses the contempt the earlier one states.
links.text_issue: 283 last line cut short; flagged uncertain

links.reason: 245 warns that seizing the king who made him will make Fortune turn (பிறழ்ந்திடும் பூ மகள்); 2323 calls the usurper's reign a Kali-rule that perished. That is a fair fulfilment, but 2323 itself does not say Fortune turned or give his deed as the cause, and teaches leans on 2314-2316 outside the packet; line 4 is flagged uncertain.

27 says that while kings bring tribute and the sceptre runs just (செங்கோல் நடப்ப) he heard the dharma and renounced; 2377 closes on peace, enemies, disease and hunger gone (பகையும் நோயும் பசியும் கெட்டு) and turns to what befell the king of kings. The peace is the height the patikam names before the turning, so the later verse sets up what the earlier announced.

550 is about a king punishing the cruel (கொலையிற் கொடியாரை) as weeding; 824 reports a lion in the forest and someone driving it off (நீக்கினான்), with the removing agent and the lion's fate obscure. A beast is not a wrongdoer and the verse does not say it was killed, so the weeding image is stretched over a hunting report.

Both verses use the same mechanism, a past deed driving a man (முனம் ஆகிய பான்மை முளைத்து; ஊழ் வினை துரத்தலானும்), so there is no incompatible claim; the note itself calls it one mechanism. 215 also gives the king's own heart as a cause (மனமாம் நெறி), so 'only the son's case adds' his own cause is not true.

1891 is a warning on hidden weapons in worshipping hands and tears (தொழுததங் கையினுள்ளும் ... அழுத கண்ணீரினுள்ளும்); it says nothing of the father or the kingdom handed to Kattiyankaran. Reading it as a lesson drawn from the family's ruin is a connection supplied by the note, not by the Tamil.

304 already gives the cause as earlier merit helping and turns his mind to a vow (புண்ணிய நோன்பு நோற்கப் பொருந்திய மனத்தன்); 308 repeats past austerity as the source of pleasure and adds weariness and the visit to Vamanan. It adds a detail but is largely the same step restated, and 308's sense is flagged uncertain.

Both verses show ponds thick with washed-off face-paste and saffron (அரிசனம் அழித்த சேற்றினும் குங்குமக் குழம்பினும்; குங்குமம் நிறைந்த ... பொய்கைகள்). The image is real but is a stock description of bathing luxury, and teaches states only the shared theme.

941 has women's composure broken by the young men's beauty (மனநிறை அழிதரு); 1254 has the woman's own admission that her restraint (நிறை) gave way to desire in public. The shared word is real, but 941 is a narrator's scene of general desire with a doubtful last line, so it does not develop the Kural's first-person claim.

1843 credits umbrellas, kings and the elephant ride to a good-deed deity (நல்வினைத் தெய்வம்); Naladiyar 3 says those who rode under the umbrella fall when other deeds wear out. The pair is apt, but 1843 says nothing of reversal and the quatrain does not assume the good-deed source, so both gains rest on the reader's juxtaposition.

689's sneer 'is he king of this city' (நன்னகர்க்கு மன்னனோ) is dramatic irony; 316's prophecy is that the child will crush the hostile king. They do not conflict, and the sneer does not voice the prophecy, only the story's irony.

153 says heaped deeds (புஞ்சிய வினைகள்) ripen at death; it names no earlier hurt by the dying pair. The note's 'king's offering returns on him' is a reconstruction from outside the verse, so the Kural's முற்பகல் செய்யின் / பிற்பகல் has no matched act in 153.

1880 gives 'he is in the heart of those who never leave him, so I will not recall him' (நெஞ்சினுள்ளார் ஆதலால் நினைத்தல் செய்யேன்), which does match 1125's logic of not needing to recall what is never forgotten. But nothing shows the epic draws on the Kural, so 'gains its source' is unsupported, and the reproach reading depends on புதுமணவாளனார் alone.

1451 foretells the husband is the man at whose sight she is suddenly ashamed (கதுமென நாணப்பட்டான், subject unclear); 1472 shows her modesty broken (உண்ணிறை நாணும் உடைந்தன) at the sight. A prophecy and its event, but the sign (feeling shame) and the event (shame breaking) do not match cleanly.

84-97 is a nun's warning to Kovalan not to step on crab and snail; 44 describes ploughmen scattering fish. The note argues from the Cintamani verse's silence about harm, which a field-scene verse would not state, so the 'epics keep the scruple for the ascetic' lesson is not in either Tamil text.

186 says the world lives by the king and it is the king's duty to know it (அறிகை ... வேந்தற்குக் கடனே); 246 says kings surpass gods in many ways (பலவும் மிக்கனர் தேவரின் பார்த்திவர்). The 'ban on the subject' and minister-warning in teaches and gains come from the rest of Dharmadattan's speech, not this verse, and 186 does not rank kings over gods.

978 has Civakan judge death better than living while a woman's life is in danger (வாழ்வின் சாதல் எண்ணினன்) and charge the elephant; 1049 has Gunamalai name service as the wage for his toil (வருத்தச்சொற் கூலியாக ... அடிப்பணி செய்வதல்லால்). Her answer is a response to that risk, not just the next scene; 'shamed life' is a slight overstatement of 978.

1965 has him ask what medicine there is for the wound and look back (மருந்தென்கொல் ... மறித்து நோக்கி), then melt; the verse does not say the look cures. The Kural's two looks (இருநோக்கு) are a different structure, and gains asserts an answer the verse does not state.

1993 has Civakan promise a return as quick as an arrow (எறிந்த கோலினே); 1151 refuses such a promise of speedy return. Vimalai's tears and the 'wordless retort' come from verse 1994, outside the packet, and the epic verse does not stage a refusal.

69 has Yugi spread news of his death and burn a body in his place (மரித்தனன் வார்த்தை); 70 reports enemy kings seizing the high lands, thinking him hidden (தன்னை உங்கரத்தலின் ... நாடு பற்றினர்). The consequence follows from the ruse and counts a cost 69 does not.

13 summarises Suramanjari's powder beaten and her vow to look on no man; 875 only shows a woman held out powder, and her identity is uncertain (the marker allows Gunamalai or a maid). The link to the vow is carried by the patikam, not by 875, and teaches is a theme remark.

251 reports the parents' animal births from swollen deeds (வீங்கிய வினைகள்); the Siddhar asks when he will say enough to births as stone, tree, fish and bird. 251 names no killing, so 'traces it to a particular killing' is not in the verse, and the two are one rebirth theme in different voices, not a qualification.

1097 likens appearing in the states of birth to waking from deep sleep (கட்டுயில் அனந்தரம் போலக் கதிகளுள் தோன்றுமாறு) and adds release, a real extension of 339's birth-as-waking. But no evidence shows Civakan draws on the couplet, so 'calm learned from the tradition' and the Kural as 'first step of a scheme' are the note's reading.

Both turn on a blessing at a sneeze (தும்மினான் ... சீவ என்றதே; வழுத்தினாள் தும்மினேன்), a distinctive shared custom. The gains are thin: the couplet's lovers' quarrel gains nothing from a name-giving scene, and the 'hidden mother' is the marker's inference.

653 is an obscure jest, with a repaired text, a five-line stanza and an inferred speaker, in which the gods hid her breasts because her eyes kill (முலைகரந்து வைத்தார்). The pairing with 1087's cloth over the breasts like an elephant's face-cloth rests on that reading, and 'the gods removed what the cloth veils' is built from it.
links.text_issue: 653 stanza 5 lines; TSCII repairs; sense flagged uncertain

links.reason: 132 says learning does not perish while its owners live (தாமுளராக் கேடின்றால்), 398 that it protects through seven births (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). The link is real, but teaches is about which commentator reads 132 closer to the Kural, a point about commentary, not the Tamil.

200 offers Pari's daughters as a suppliant and brahmin (பரிசிலன் மன்னும் அந்தணன்); 201 offers them as the father's friend and brahmin poet (தந்தை தோழன் ... அந்தணன், புலவன்). The comparison is informative, but 201 does not extend 200 (both claim அந்தணன்), so the two are parallel offers to different kings.

2366 narrates a god's crowning of Civakan; it states no ranking, and the epic proceeds to renunciation. 1601 ranks the 'feet kings' above crowned ones (முடிமன்னர் / அடிமன்னர்), but the Cintamani verse never claims the crown is the highest state, so there is no incompatible claim.

203 gives the dilemma that the passing power is a sixth beyond the five or else total destruction (ஆறாகாவோ ... முழுக்கேடு); 580 turns the lac-and-seed analogy the same way, asking for a further thing beyond the five (ஐந்திற்கும் வேறொன்று காட்டாய்). Both are Neelakesi's Jain argument against Buddhist views, and the note keeps them as hers.

377 laments that the nectar ending birth is rarely won (ஆர் அமிர்து அரிதில் பெற்றாம்); 2749 says a human birth is rarer than a pole meeting a yoke-hole (மானிடம் பெறலே அரிது). The rare things differ (the teaching versus the birth), so 'the earlier complaint is given its measure' conflates them.

1329 has the man wish the sulk would last so he can plead; 2509 has Civakan blame an old sin for her tears and bid the bees plead for him. No claim is contradicted: it is a lover's figure of speech versus a wish, and 'a stage he has not yet found pleasing' is not in the verse.

68 says the low's anger spreads and never dies (நீசர் வெகுளி ... பரக்கும்); 111 has the low-born rise even against those who part the fighters (விலக்குவார் மேலும் எழுதல்). The fit is plausible, but 111 does not name anger and its closing proverb is obscure (flagged), so the concrete 'path' is partly inferred.

Both give the evening and its sounds as burning (புகையிற் பொங்கழல் போற்சுடுகின்றவே; அழல்போலும் மாலை, குழல்). The claim that Padumai is not yet joined or parted is not in the verse, and 'the source convention of its list' asserts a debt the Tamil does not show.

1864 orders a drum proclaimed for a festival (முரசறைக என்றான்); 1868 shows the proclamation and the city rejoicing. This is plot sequence, and the 'authority at its greatest before the turning away' goes beyond what either verse says.

2824 lists lying, killing, theft and lust as what ascetics guard against (பொய் கொலை களவு காமம்); 2868 gives the killing of life as a fault to a prince, and the marker says its list differs (another's wife, deceit-wealth). It is the same ethic stated for two classes, but 2868 here shows only killing, so 'the four sins given to a layman' overstates it.

1499 offers the choice to live in service or leave the body (உடம்பு ஒழித்து ஏகுவேனோ), a lover's hyperbole like 1124's life and death on her presence. The epic's own going-away is the later event of 1505, so 'the parting he chooses' and 'seen from the side of the one who goes' are not in 1499, where the going is dying.
